strengths: The paper supports a useful empirical contribution suitable for Findings: lightweight probes of question representations can predict short-answer QA correctness before answer generation. This is relevant to efficient reliability assessment of LLMs.

The evaluation covers four main LLMs and three datasets, with additional HotpotQA and Gemma experiments. Comparisons include prompting, attention-based probing, LoRA, and full fine-tuning. FacLens generally achieves competitive or better AUROC with substantially lower reported training costs.

The transfer experiments provide meaningful evidence beyond the motivational argument. For example, LLaMA2-to-Mistral adaptation on NQ improves AUROC from 0.461 to 0.693, approaching the target-supervised result of 0.714. The question-aligned batching ablation also supports that design choice.

The method is straightforward, and the manuscript supplies model identifiers, dataset filtering and splits, decoding choices, architecture, optimization settings, and a code link. These provide a reasonable basis for reproducing the core supervised experiments.
weaknesses: Section 4.2 does not establish the claimed absence of concept shift. A pooled classifier can infer model identity from domain-separated representations and implement different mappings for different LLMs. Consequently, matching individual-model performance and predictions does not demonstrate equal cross-domain P(y|X). AUROC also cannot establish equality of conditional probabilities, and the supervised t-SNE visualization is not independent evidence. The empirical transfer results remain useful, but the stronger explanation should be withdrawn or substantially qualified.

The reported 97% label accuracy is insufficiently justified. Footnote 4 audits only 240 negative, meaning factual, examples and assumes all positive labels are correct. A response without a gold-answer substring can nevertheless express a correct paraphrase or unlisted alias. Both label classes require auditing before making this accuracy claim or interpreting the labels as reliable measures of factuality.

The transfer comparison omits an especially relevant baseline: train a probe on target-model representations using the source-model labels for the same questions. This would test whether MMD adds value beyond transferring correlated question-level correctness labels. Directly applying a probe across unaligned hidden coordinates is a weak comparison. Controls using independent question embeddings would also help distinguish model-specific knowledge signals from general question difficulty.

Some experimental details limit reproducibility and confidence in small improvements. The label-free checkpoint-selection procedure for adaptation is unspecified, while Figures 7 and 13 show target-test performance throughout training. The manuscript should clarify selection without implying that these plots themselves prove leakage. Random seeds, repeated-run variability, and confidence intervals are also missing.

The evidence supports benchmark correctness ranking more strongly than calibrated knowledge awareness or deployment benefits. Main experiments use random splits within filtered datasets and greedy decoding; NQ contains only 1,244 questions. Calibration, risk–coverage evaluation, and stronger distribution-shift tests would substantiate the broader claims. Together with the unsupported concept-shift interpretation, these limitations weaken the case for main-conference publication.
